title: Store footfall
intro: A short work sample. Answer in your own words, the way you would explain it to a manager.
question: Did the store perform better in Week 2? What would you investigate next?

answer_key.verdict: No. Purchases rose in total, but a smaller share of visitors bought something.

values.change: Down 5 percentage points, a 20% relative drop

answer_key.interpretation: Visitors grew about 33% but purchases grew only about 7%, so a smaller share of visitors bought in Week 2.
recommendation_examples_valid: Check whether popular items were out of stock in Week 2.
Check checkout queues or staffing at busy times.
Check whether a promotion or local event brought in visitors who were only browsing.
Check whether the footfall counter changed or double-counted visitors.

recommendation_examples_invalid.why: Contradicts the data. More visitors already came with a lower purchase rate.
Not proportionate. A drastic step before anyone knows the cause.

recommendation_examples_invalid.text: Check online reviews of the brand.
recommendation_examples_invalid.why: Not linked to the change in the purchase rate.

answer_key.note: Valid examples are illustrations, not the only correct answers.

metric_calculation.nudge: Both columns went up. Is comparing totals a fair way to judge the two weeks when the number of visitors changed?
metric_calculation.hint: For each week, work out what fraction of store visitors made a purchase. Then compare the two weeks.

interpretation.nudge: What does your comparison say about how well the store turned visitors into buyers?
interpretation.hint: Ask yourself whether purchases grew at the same pace as visitors, and what that says about the store.

recommendation.nudge: What could cause the change you found in the numbers, and how would you check it this week?
recommendation.hint: Think of one thing that could cause a smaller share of visitors to buy, and how you would check it this week.
